notes.meaning: God calls His people to sing out with joy because He is their strength and defender. He protected their forefather Jacob, and He faithfully carries His people through every trial. Wholehearted and lively praise is the right response to all He has done.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine applied the name Asaph to the gathered Christian church, teaching that believers should rejoice with loud voices even when human words cannot fully express their praise.

notes.meaning: Worship is meant to be full of joyful music, combining voices with drums and stringed instruments. The temple musicians were called to bring their sweetest instruments to praise the Lord with all their skill. God wants His people to serve Him with glad hearts rather than gloomy duty.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw a spiritual picture here, teaching that the tambourine made of animal skin means believers who receive spiritual truth should give back material help to others.

notes.meaning: The priests were commanded to blow the ram's horn to mark the start of the month and to announce the big feast days. This blast served as a sacred call for the whole nation to gather for worship. It reminded the people of God's covenant and summoned them to joyful celebration.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted the new moon as the believer's new life in Christ, so sounding the horn represents preaching the gospel boldly.

notes.meaning: Israel did not invent these feast days on their own. God Himself gave these rules to Jacob's family as a lasting law. True worship is grounded in what God commands, not in human tradition or invention.

God set up this celebration as a lasting reminder for the nation of Israel, here called Joseph. It marked their march out of Egypt, where they had lived among foreigners whose speech and worship were alien to them. Remembering how hard their slavery was made God's rescue shine even brighter.

The Lord Himself reminds Israel that He lifted the crushing loads of forced labour from their backs. He freed their hands from the heavy baskets used to carry clay and bricks. Their freedom was not won by their own strength, but was a gracious gift of God.

When the Israelites cried out in misery, the Lord answered them with mighty power from the stormy thundercloud at the Red Sea. Later, at the waters of Meribah, He tested their faith when they were thirsty and complained. Even when they failed the test, God still showed them His patience and mercy.

God asks His people to stop and listen carefully to His warning. He has faithfully answered their prayers, and now He expects them to heed His guidance. Real worship requires obedient listening, not just singing songs.

The central rule of God's covenant was that His people must never worship false gods or bow down to foreign idols. The Lord alone is the living God, and He will not share His glory with anything made by human hands. Loyalty to God requires casting away every rival.

Because the Lord proved His love and power by rescuing Israel from Egypt, He asks them to trust Him completely. He tells them to open their mouths wide, like hungry young birds waiting to be fed, and promises to supply every real need. God has limitless blessings ready for those who come to Him in faithful prayer.

Despite all God had done, Israel refused to listen to His voice or submit to His rule. God was ready to be their God, but they did not want to be His obedient people. Their failure came from willful rebellion, not from a lack of light or invitation.

When Israel insisted on rebelling, God gave them over to the stubborn desires of their own hearts. He stepped back and removed His restraining grace, letting them follow their own foolish choices into trouble. Being left to our own sinful desires is one of the most sobering judgments God can bring.

The Lord expresses tender longing and sorrow over His people, wishing they had listened to Him and walked in His ways. God takes no pleasure in the ruin of sinners and grieves over the harm they bring upon themselves. Obedience would have opened the door to lasting peace and safety.

differ.view: John Gill taught that God's wish reveals what He commands and approves of in His creatures, rather than an unfulfilled divine decree.
Adam Clarke emphasized the words as expressing genuine, deep-seated divine grief over Israel's self-inflicted ruin.

notes.meaning: If Israel had stayed faithful, God would have quickly defeated all their enemies with ease. Sin was the true reason their troubles dragged on and their rescue was delayed. When God's people walk in holiness, He fights their battles for them.

Had Israel walked with God, their enemies would have cowered before them and yielded, even if only out of fear. In the traditional Protestant reading, the phrase means Israel's own blessed prosperity would have lasted forever. Disobedience robbed them of a peace that could have endured through every generation.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine understood the lasting time to refer to the eternal punishment and doom awaiting God's enemies.

notes.meaning: God longed to satisfy His people with the very best grain and with wild honey stored in rock crevices. These rich gifts show that God delights to provide both daily bread and deep joy to those who trust Him. Christian writers often see these gifts as pointing to Christ, the true Bread of life who satisfies the soul.
